newsitem.title: CHINA: China H2 copper imports seen down, reserve casts pall.
newsitem.headline: China H2 copper imports seen down, reserve casts pall.

text.p: China's copper imports in the second half of 1997 could slide due to oversupply, but the government's unclear buying intentions have cast a shadow over the market, Chinese analysts said on Wednesday.
With domestic supply now far exceeding demand, China's copper production would slow and the surplus should shrink as the year progressed, Shanghai Colub Consultants Co said.

As copper prices fall to levels suitable for China's State Strategic Reserve Bureau (SSRB), the government's secretive stock buying arm, its next move on the market remained unclear, Shanghai Colub, a private think tank, said in an internal report.
China, as a net copper importer, is a major swing factor in the market. The official China Daily on Tuesday put 1997 consumption at 1.1 million tonnes, with production at 950,000 tonnes.
Recent annual imports have been around 300,000 tonnes. China is considered a savvy price-buyer and the market braces itself when London Metal Exchange (LME) copper prices dip.
China reportedly bought 300,000 tonnes of copper on the world market on price dips in late 1996, which saw the country enter 1997 with a central stockpile of up to 270,000 tonnes.
Western analysts have said China is not likely to buy this year, if at all, until the price drops to $2,200 a tonne or below.
LME copper is currently hovering just below the market resistance point of $2,300 a tonne, a level Colub's analysts said was suitable for China's central reserve.

"Now the copper price is back to the level of the beginning of 1997 when the SSRB put together its procurement plan," Colub's report said. "So we think it is reasonable that its procurement plan will be carried out."
Chinese strategic reserve information is a state secret.

Colub's report gave no details of the SSRB's buying plan. But it cited current LME prices, foreign reserves of $121.2 billion at the end of June, and stable economic growth as the basis of its prediction.
Chinese imports of copper and copper products in the past five months totalled 260,000 tonnes, an increase of 7.7 percent compared with same year-ago period, Colub said.
Scrap imports were 277,000 tonnes and concentrate imports 410,000 tonnes, up 15.8 percent and 25.2 percent respectively, Colub said.
Refined copper production in first-half 1997 rose 13.1 percent on first-half 1996 to 503,000 tonnes, it said.

Coupled with a carried-over inventory of 200,000 tonnes, "it is obvious that copper supply surpasses demand, which is also reflected in the price plunges on the Shanghai Metal Exchange (SHME)," the report said.
Prices on the SHME have whipsawed lately as local producers watching world price falls have rushed to lock in profits.

While they do mostly follow LME movements, the SHME copper prices also to a large extent reflect local fundamentals and have fallen to 20,550 yuan on Wednesday from above 24,000 yuan ($2,891) per tonne in March.
Physical prices have also fallen, to Wednesday's 20,600 yuan, reflecting a slowdown in demand, a lack of cash and ample market supply, local and Western traders said.
Colub's report said the only recent buyer of copper futures on the SHME was a floor broker representing the SSRB who had accumulated a total long position of 30,000 tonnes.
Other trading sources in Shanghai have also said the SSRB was buying through floor brokers on open interest.
"Though this does not necessarily mean that the SSRB is buying copper, its market behaviour is self-evident," Colub said.
-- Shanghai Newsroom (8621) 6279-8544
